courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Using a free tool (Trello, or just a plain doc) set up two side-by-side artifacts: a Waterfall-style phase list (Requirements -> Design -> Build -> Test -> Deploy) for a small made-up database change, and a Scrum sprint backlog of 5 self-written user stories in proper "As a [user], I want [goal], so that [reason]" format for that same change. Feel the structural difference between planning it all up front versus breaking it into a backlog.
slots.deliverable: A side-by-side Waterfall phase list and a 5-story Scrum sprint backlog written in correct user-story format, saved as a doc or shared Trello board link.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Kanban board (Trello, GitHub Projects, or Azure DevOps Boards are all free) with columns Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Code Review, Done. Add the 5 user stories from the previous slot as cards, then drag 2 of them through every column to feel how a work-in-progress limit and a blocked card behave. Label each card with which SDLC environment (Dev, QA, UAT, or Production) it would be sitting in while it occupies that column.
slots.deliverable: A live Kanban board (screenshot or shareable link) with 5 labeled cards, at least 2 of which have been moved through every column from Backlog to Done.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git if it isn't already on your machine, create a local repository, and run the real everyday workflow end to end: git init, add a file, git add, git commit -m with a proper descriptive message, git checkout -b to branch, make a second change, commit it, and (if you have a GitHub account) push both the main and feature branch and open a pull request. Then sketch a one-page CI/CD pipeline diagram (Commit -> Build -> Test -> Deploy) naming a real tool at each stage, such as GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or Azure Pipelines.
slots.deliverable: A local or pushed Git repository with at least 2 commits and 1 feature branch, plus a one-page CI/CD pipeline diagram naming a real tool at each of its 4 stages.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the capstone simulation, then act as if you've just been assigned a real ticket: write out the full lifecycle of one feature request by hand, start to finish. Write its user story, break it into 3 sub-tasks on a Kanban board, name the Git branch you'd create for it with 2 realistic commit messages, write one QA test note someone would log against it, and state which CI/CD stage it would pass through before it reaches Production.
slots.deliverable: A single written walkthrough document tracing one feature request through its user story, 3 Kanban sub-tasks, a Git branch name with 2 commit messages, a QA test note, and the CI/CD stages leading to Production.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a condensed one-person 'sprint' that chains everything in this course together: pick 3 small, real improvements you could make to any personal or practice project, write each as a proper user story, put all 3 on the Kanban board from the second slot, create one Git branch per story and commit real work to each, move each card all the way to Done, and finish with a 3-sentence sprint retrospective covering what went well, what didn't, and one change for next sprint.
slots.deliverable: 3 completed user stories each with its own Git branch and commits, all 3 Kanban cards moved to Done, and a written 3-sentence sprint retrospective.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can speak the shared working language of a real IT department — writing a proper user story, running a Kanban board through to Done, using Git's everyday branch-commit-push-pull-request workflow, and tracing a single change through Dev, QA, UAT, and a CI/CD pipeline into Production.
